Both things are true and neither cancels the other. They worked themselves half to death — that's real, and it cost them something. And you were twelve and nothing you had was yours. Their exhaustion explains how it happened. It doesn't erase what it did to you. You're allowed to hold both without it being a verdict on them.

The reason it sounds like complaining is that you've only ever heard it framed as an accusation. There's another version, and it's not about them at all — it's a fact about you. *I grew up being the one who kept things running, and I learned not to put my name on anything.* That sentence doesn't say your parents were bad. It doesn't say they didn't work hard. It says what you learned, which is true regardless of why.

And notice what just happened: you're protecting their reputation at the cost of being able to explain yourself to the person you live with. That's the same move as the bag. Making yourself smaller so nobody has to feel uncomfortable. You've been doing it so long it feels like loyalty instead of what it is.

He doesn't need the whole story. He needs one sentence that makes the car make sense. Something like: *"I grew up where nothing was really mine and I was the one holding it together. So when I say I'm not taking it back, that's what it's about — not you."* That's it. He can ask more later, or not.

You don't have to decide tonight. But if you want the car to land as something other than sudden, he needs a door to walk through, and that's the door.
